title: Hampi at a glance
content: Hampi is a village in the Vijayanagara district of Karnataka, on the southern bank of the Tungabhadra river. It sits inside the ruins of Vijayanagara, the capital of the Vijayanagara Empire. The Group of Monuments at Hampi was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986. The landscape is known for its piles of granite boulders, banana plantations and paddy fields, with temples, palaces, markets and waterworks spread over a wide area. The nearest large town and railway station is Hosapete (Hospet), roughly 13 km away.

title: History of Vijayanagara
content: The Vijayanagara Empire was founded in 1336 by the brothers Harihara I and Bukka Raya I of the Sangama dynasty. Its capital, Vijayanagara, grew into one of the largest and richest cities of its time, visited and described by Persian and Portuguese travellers. The empire reached its height under Krishnadevaraya of the Tuluva dynasty, who ruled from 1509 to 1529 and commissioned or expanded many of the grandest monuments. In 1565 the empire's army was defeated at the Battle of Talikota by an alliance of Deccan sultanates, and the capital was plundered and largely abandoned. The ruins seen today are what remains of that city.

title: Why Hampi matters
content: Hampi is historically important as the last great Hindu imperial capital of South India and as one of the best-preserved medieval city sites in the world. UNESCO recognises it for its Dravidian temple architecture, its fusion with Indo-Islamic styles in royal buildings such as the Lotus Mahal and Elephant Stables, its sophisticated water management with tanks, aqueducts and channels, and the way the city was planned around the natural boulder landscape. It also remains a living religious centre, with worship continuing at the Virupaksha Temple.

title: How Hampi is laid out
content: Hampi is easiest to explore as zones. The Sacred Centre around Hampi Bazaar holds the Virupaksha Temple, Hemakuta Hill, the monolithic Ganesha statues, the Krishna Temple and the Lakshmi Narasimha statue. The riverside trail runs north-east past Kodandarama Temple and the Achyutaraya Temple to the Vittala Temple complex. The Royal Centre to the south, towards Kamalapura, includes the Royal Enclosure with the Mahanavami Dibba and Stepped Tank, the Hazara Rama Temple, the Zenana Enclosure with the Lotus Mahal, the Elephant Stables and the Queen's Bath. Across the Tungabhadra on the north bank are Anegundi village, Anjanadri Hill, Pampa Sarovar, Sanapur Lake and Virupapur Gaddi.

title: Getting around Hampi
content: Distances between Hampi's zones are several kilometres, so most visitors combine walking with auto-rickshaws, rented bicycles, mopeds or electric scooters. Walking is practical within the Sacred Centre and along the riverside trail to Vittala Temple, which takes about an hour at an easy pace. Battery-operated vehicles carry visitors between the Vittala car park and the temple. Crossing to the north bank (Anegundi, Virupapur Gaddi, Sanapur) is by small ferry or coracle when the river allows, or by road via a longer detour. Ferries stop in the evening and are suspended when the river is high.

title: Climate and best time to visit
content: Hampi has a hot, semi-arid climate. The most comfortable months are from October to February, when days are warm and evenings mild. March to May is very hot, with afternoon temperatures commonly near or above 38°C, and many sites have little shade. The south-west monsoon brings rain between June and September; the river can rise sharply, which affects coracle rides and ferry crossings. Starting early in the morning, resting indoors in the midday heat and returning for sunset is the usual rhythm.

title: Temple etiquette and dress
content: Remove footwear before entering temples and shrines; shoe stands are usually available near the entrance. Dress modestly with shoulders and knees covered, especially at active temples such as Virupaksha. Photography may be restricted inside the sanctum of active temples, so follow the signs and ask before photographing worshippers or priests. Do not climb on carvings, pillars or monuments, and do not tap the musical pillars at Vittala Temple, which are protected. Hampi is a temple town: alcohol and meat are generally not served in the village around the bazaar.

title: Practical tips
content: Carry plenty of water, sun protection and a hat; shade is scarce at many sites. Wear comfortable shoes that are easy to remove for temples. Cash is useful because small shops, ferries and coracle operators may not accept cards, and ATMs are limited in the village itself. The ASI ticket bought at the Vittala Temple is also valid the same day at the Zenana Enclosure and Elephant Stables. Many open-air sites can be visited without a ticket. Allow at least two full days to see the main zones without rushing.

title: Religious landscape and legends
content: The Virupaksha Temple honours Shiva as Virupaksha, the consort of the local river goddess Pampa, and the area is also known as Pampa Kshetra. The region around Anegundi on the north bank is traditionally identified with Kishkindha, the monkey kingdom of the Ramayana, and Anjanadri Hill is revered as the birthplace of Hanuman. Many carvings across Hampi, notably on the walls of the Hazara Rama Temple, depict scenes from the Ramayana.

title: Architecture of Hampi
content: Vijayanagara temples are known for tall entrance gateways called gopurams, pillared halls (mandapas) with finely carved composite pillars, and long colonnaded bazaar streets leading to temple entrances, as at Hampi Bazaar, Krishna Bazaar and the Sule Bazaar of the Achyutaraya Temple. Royal and civic buildings such as the Lotus Mahal, Elephant Stables and Queen's Bath combine these traditions with Indo-Islamic arches and domes. Giant monolithic sculptures, including the Lakshmi Narasimha statue and the Ganesha statues on Hemakuta Hill, were carved directly from boulders.

title: Food in and around Hampi
content: Food in Hampi village is mostly vegetarian South Indian and North Indian fare, including thalis, dosas and simple rice meals, along with cafes serving travellers. Because Hampi is a temple town, alcohol and non-vegetarian food are generally not available around the bazaar; Kamalapura and Hosapete have a wider choice. Restaurant opening times vary and are best checked locally or with a live search.

title: Hampi with children or older travellers
content: Families generally find the Royal Centre easy going: the Zenana Enclosure, Elephant Stables, Stepped Tank and Queen's Bath are close together on mostly level ground. The Vittala Temple has battery vehicles from the car park, and coracle rides are popular with children when the river is calm. Hill climbs such as Matanga Hill and Anjanadri Hill involve steep steps or scrambling and suit only fit walkers. Plan around the midday heat and carry water.
